svg.title: ΔG°, K and E° are one number in three costumes
svg.desc: A triangle links the three quantities. Standard free energy change sits at the top, the equilibrium constant at the lower left and the standard cell potential at the lower right. The left edge carries the relation that the standard free energy change equals minus the gas constant times temperature times the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant, which at 298 kelvin is minus 5.71 kilojoules per mole times the base-ten logarithm of the equilibrium constant. The right edge carries the relation that the standard free energy change equals minus the number of electrons times the Faraday constant times the standard cell potential, with the Faraday constant equal to 96.5 kilojoules per volt per mole. The bottom edge links potential and equilibrium constant directly: the standard potential equals 0.0592 volts divided by the number of electrons times the base-ten logarithm of the equilibrium constant at 298 kelvin. Inside the triangle a sign rule records that a negative standard free energy change corresponds to an equilibrium constant greater than one and a positive standard potential, and that all three flip together. Below, a ruler plots the standard free energy change against the equilibrium constant on a logarithmic scale, marked at plus 17.1, plus 11.4, plus 5.7, zero, minus 5.7, minus 11.4, minus 17.1 and minus 30.5 kilojoules per mole, corresponding to equilibrium constants of one thousandth, one hundredth, one tenth, one, ten, one hundred, one thousand and about two hundred thousand, with ATP hydrolysis marked at the last of these. Each 5.7 kilojoules per mole is worth exactly one factor of ten. A panel distinguishes the chemical standard state, where every solute is at one molar including hydrogen ion, meaning pH zero, from the biochemical standard state written with a prime, where hydrogen ion is fixed at ten to the minus seven molar, meaning pH seven, and water is treated as a pure liquid; biochemical tables use the primed convention, which is why the free energy of ATP hydrolysis is quoted as minus 30.5 kilojoules per mole. A second panel works the coupling arithmetic: glucose plus phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate is plus 13.8 kilojoules per mole on its own, ATP hydrolysis is minus 30.5, and because free energy is a state function the two add to minus 16.7 for the reaction hexokinase actually catalyses; the catch is that the reactions must share a mechanism, since merely mixing them in one beaker couples nothing.
svg.text: ΔG°, K and E° are one number in three costumes
Know any one of them and you know the other two. The MCAT moves between them constantly — the conversions are worth more than the derivations.
ΔG° < 0 ⟺ K > 1 ⟺ E° > 0 ⟺ products favoured at
equilibrium. Change the sign of any one and all three
ΔG° (kJ/mol) — and the K it implies at 298 K
every 5.7 kJ/mol is exactly one factor of ten in K
Two standard states — check which one a table uses
Chemical ΔG°: every solute at 1 M, H⁺ included — which means pH
0. Biochemical ΔG°′: H⁺ fixed at 10⁻⁷ M (pH 7) and water treated
as a pure liquid. Biochemistry tables use the primed version,
which is where −30.5 kJ/mol for ATP comes from.
Coupling: the arithmetic, and the catch
They add because G is a state function — but only if the two
share a mechanism. Two reactions in one beaker are not
The distinction every one of these questions is really testing
ΔG° is a fixed number that fixes K. ΔG is where the reaction stands right now, and ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K). A reaction with
ΔG° = +30 kJ/mol runs forward quite happily whenever the cell holds Q far below K — which is exactly what a pathway does by
And the one that is not about thermodynamics at all
ΔG < 0 says a reaction may happen, never that it will happen soon. Diamond is thermodynamically unstable at room temperature. An
enzyme changes the rate by lowering the activation barrier and changes ΔG, ΔG° and K by exactly nothing.
